subject: integrated-science
title: Integrated Science MYP 5 eAssessment Structure Mock B (8 tasks, 75 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1 | A 6]]
Sodium and chlorine react to make sodium chloride. Sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23.
(a) State the number of neutrons in an atom of sodium. (1 mark)
(b) State the electron arrangement of a sodium atom. (1 mark)
(c) Explain why sodium is placed in Group 1 of the periodic table. (1 mark)
(d) Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. State what is meant by the term isotope. (1 mark)
(e) In a sample of chlorine, 75% of the atoms are chlorine-35 and 25% are chlorine-37. Calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine. (2 marks)

Total for Question 1: 6 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons [1]. (b) 2,8,1 [1]. (c) It has one electron in its outer shell (accept: it forms ions with a 1+ charge) [1]. (d) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons [1]. (e) (75 x 35 + 25 x 37) / 100 [1] = 35.5 [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 2 | A 7]]
A cyclist and bicycle have a combined mass of 80 kg and are travelling at 6.0 m/s along a level road. The cyclist brakes and the bicycle comes to rest in 4.0 s.
(a) Calculate the kinetic energy of the cyclist and bicycle before braking. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the deceleration of the bicycle, assuming it is constant. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the resultant force that acts on the bicycle while it is slowing down. (1 mark)
(d) Explain what happens to the kinetic energy as the bicycle slows down. (2 marks)

Total for Question 2: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) KE = 1/2 x m x v² = 0.5 x 80 x 6.0² [1] = 1440 J [1]. (b) a = change in speed / time = (6.0 - 0) / 4.0 [1] = 1.5 m/s² [1]. (c) F = m x a = 80 x 1.5 = 120 N [1] (error carried forward from (b)). (d) The kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy (heat) in the brakes, tyres and road [1]; energy is conserved, so the total energy stays the same but is spread out into the surroundings and is not useful [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 3 | A 7]]
Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli of the lungs.
(a) Name the gas that diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood. (1 mark)
(b) Describe two features of the alveoli that make gas exchange efficient. (2 marks)
(c) Explain why a person's breathing rate increases during exercise. (2 marks)
(d) Describe the movement of the diaphragm and the effect on the chest during inhalation. (2 marks)

Total for Question 3: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Oxygen [1]. (b) Any two from: walls are one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short; very large total surface area from millions of alveoli; covered by a dense network of capillaries which maintains the concentration gradient; moist surface so gases dissolve [1][1]. (c) The muscles respire faster and produce more carbon dioxide, which is detected by the brain [1]; breathing faster gets oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide more quickly [1]. (d) The diaphragm contracts and moves down (flattens) [1]; the volume of the chest increases and the pressure falls, so air is drawn into the lungs [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 4 | A 7]]
Indigestion is caused by too much hydrochloric acid in the stomach. Indigestion tablets contain magnesium hydroxide, which neutralises the acid.
(a) State the pH of a neutral solution. (1 mark)
(b) State the colour of universal indicator in a strong acid. (1 mark)
(c) Write a word equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. (1 mark)
(d) Balance the equation for the reaction between magnesium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid: Mg(OH)2 + HCl -> MgCl2 + H2O (2 marks)
(e) Suggest why sodium hydroxide solution would not be used in an indigestion remedy. (1 mark)
(f) Name the type of reaction between an acid and a base. (1 mark)

Total for Question 4: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) pH 7 [1]. (b) Red [1]. (c) Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride + water [1]. (d) Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O: coefficient 2 before HCl [1]; coefficient 2 before H2O [1]. (e) It is a strong alkali that is corrosive and would damage the stomach and throat [1]. (f) Neutralisation [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 5 | B 10]]
A student wants to find out how the length of a simple pendulum affects the time it takes to swing. A small metal bob hangs from a thread tied to a clamp. The student pulls the bob a short distance to one side, releases it, and times the swings with a stopwatch.
(a) State a research question that this investigation could answer. (2 marks)
(b) Formulate a testable hypothesis, using scientific reasoning. (2 marks)
(c) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable. (2 marks)
(d) Describe how the student can obtain an accurate value for the time of one swing, and measure the length. (2 marks)
(e) Outline one variable that must be controlled. (1 mark)
(f) Outline one safety precaution for this investigation. (1 mark)

Total for Question 5: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) A question linking both variables, for example: How does the length of a pendulum affect the time taken for one complete swing (the period)? [2] (1 mark if both variables are named but not linked). (b) A prediction, for example: a longer pendulum will take longer for each swing [1]; with reasoning, for example: the bob has further to travel along a longer arc, and the restoring force acts more slowly (accept: a longer pendulum has a larger period because the bob travels a longer path) [1]. (c) Independent: length of the thread [1]; dependent: time for one swing (period) [1]. (d) Time 20 swings and divide by 20, which reduces the effect of reaction time [1]; measure the length with a metre rule from the clamp to the centre of the bob [1]. (e) Any one from: mass of the bob, starting angle (the same small release angle), same bob and thread [1]. (f) Any one from: make sure the clamp stand is secure so it cannot fall; keep the area clear so no one trips; wear eye protection [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 6 | C 10]]
A student adds zinc powder to 50 cm³ of copper sulfate solution of concentration 0.50 mol/dm³ in an insulated cup and records the highest temperature rise. The reaction is zinc + copper sulfate -> zinc sulfate + copper.
Mass of zinc in g: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5
Temperature rise in degrees Celsius: 4.8, 9.6, 14.1, 15.4, 15.4
(a) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and give evidence from the data. (1 mark)
(b) Describe the trend in the temperature rise as the mass of zinc increases. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the mass of zinc that reacts with all of the copper sulfate. The relative atomic mass of zinc is 65. The equation shows that 1 mol of zinc reacts with 1 mol of copper sulfate. (3 marks)
(d) Use your answer to (c) to explain the trend between 2.0 g and 2.5 g of zinc. (1 mark)
(e) Use the data to determine the temperature rise expected with 0.75 g of zinc. (1 mark)
(f) Evaluate one limitation of the method and suggest an improvement. (2 marks)

Total for Question 6: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Exothermic, because the temperature rises [1]. (b) The temperature rise increases as the mass of zinc increases, roughly in direct proportion at first (about 9.6 degrees Celsius per gram up to 1.5 g) [1]; it then levels off at 15.4 degrees Celsius and does not increase further [1]. (c) Amount of copper sulfate = 0.050 dm³ x 0.50 mol/dm³ = 0.025 mol [1]; 1 : 1 ratio so 0.025 mol of zinc is needed [1]; mass = 0.025 x 65 = 1.6 g (1.625 g) [1]. (d) All of the copper sulfate has already reacted (it is the limiting reactant) when 1.6 g of zinc has been added, so extra zinc cannot react and release more energy [1]. (e) 7.2 degrees Celsius (midway between 4.8 and 9.6; accept values from 7.0 to 7.4) [1]. (f) A limitation, for example heat is lost to the surroundings, so the temperature rises are lower than the true values (accept: zinc powder may react at different speeds, or the thermometer reading is only to 0.1 degrees Celsius) [1]; an improvement, for example use a lid on the cup, or a thicker layer of insulation, and stir the mixture [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 7 | D 10]]
Read the passage.
Clothes made from polyester and nylon shed tiny plastic fibres, called microplastics, each time they are washed. Wastewater treatment plants remove most of the fibres, but the rest are carried into rivers and the sea. Small animals such as shellfish and plankton eat them, and the fibres can carry harmful chemicals. Filters that fit inside washing machines can catch most of the fibres, but they cost money and must be emptied regularly. Some governments are considering a law that requires filters in all new machines. Manufacturers say this will make machines more expensive.
(a) Outline how microplastic fibres can enter a food chain and reach humans. (2 marks)
(b) Describe two ways of reducing the release of microplastic fibres from laundry. (2 marks)
(c) Discuss one economic factor and one political factor that affect how this problem is solved. (4 marks)
(d) Suggest and justify one action that should be taken first. (2 marks)

Total for Question 7: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Fibres are eaten by small organisms such as plankton and shellfish [1]; these are eaten by fish and other animals, and the fibres move up the food chain to humans who eat seafood [1]. (b) Any two from: fit filters to washing machines; wash clothes less often or with full loads at a lower temperature; choose natural fabrics instead of synthetic ones; improve filtering at wastewater plants [1][1]. (c) Economic: filters raise the cost of machines and need emptying, so consumers or manufacturers may resist [1]; developed, for example, poorer households may not be able to afford new machines, or the long-term cost of cleaning up the sea is higher than the cost of the filters [1]. Political: a law would force all manufacturers to fit filters [1]; developed, for example, governments must balance public pressure for the environment against pressure from industry, and laws need international agreement because rivers and seas cross borders [1]. (d) A sensible action [1] with justification, for example require filters in new machines because this stops the fibres at source and is more effective than cleaning up the sea afterwards [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 8 | A 7 | C 7 | D 4]]
A school plans to heat water for its sports-hall showers using a solar thermal panel. The panel has an area of 4.0 square metres. The average sunlight energy arriving at the panel is 600 W for each square metre, and the panel transfers 55% of this to the water. The tank holds 150 kg of water, which must be heated from 15 degrees Celsius to 45 degrees Celsius. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg degrees Celsius. Energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change.
(a) Describe how energy from the Sun is transferred to the water in the tank. (3 marks)
(b) Explain why the panel surface is black and the pipes are made of copper. (2 marks)
(c) Show that the useful power transferred to the water is 1320 W. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate the energy needed to heat the water in the tank. (3 marks)
(e) Calculate the time needed to heat the water, in hours. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (2 marks)
(f) Bacteria that cause Legionnaires' disease multiply fastest in water at temperatures between about 20 and 45 degrees Celsius and are killed above 60 degrees Celsius. The system is heated to above 60 degrees Celsius once a week. Explain how this heating kills the bacteria. (2 marks)
(g) The school could instead use a gas boiler. Evaluate the two heating systems and recommend one. (4 marks)

Total for Question 8: 18 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Energy travels from the Sun to the panel by radiation (electromagnetic waves, infrared and visible light) [1]; the panel absorbs the radiation and the pipes are heated; thermal energy passes through the pipe wall to the water by conduction [1]; the warm water rises and circulates through the tank by convection, so the whole tank is heated [1]. (b) Black surfaces are good absorbers of radiation (and poor reflectors) [1]; copper is a good conductor of thermal energy, so heat passes quickly to the water [1]. (c) Power arriving = 600 x 4.0 = 2400 W [1]; useful power = 0.55 x 2400 = 1320 W [1]. (d) Temperature change = 45 - 15 = 30 degrees Celsius [1]; energy = 150 x 4200 x 30 [1] = 18 900 000 J (18.9 MJ) [1]. (e) Time = energy / power = 18 900 000 / 1320 = 14 318 s [1]; 14 318 / 3600 = 4.0 hours [1]. (f) Bacterial cells contain enzymes, which are proteins [1]; above 60 degrees Celsius the enzymes' shape changes (they denature), so the bacteria can no longer respire or grow and they die [1]. (g) Solar: no fuel cost or carbon dioxide emissions in use, and it uses a renewable source [1]; but it is only available when the Sun shines, so the 4.0 hours of heating needs good weather and the installation costs a lot [1]. Gas boiler: heats on demand at any time, but burns a fossil fuel, producing carbon dioxide that adds to climate change and costs more to run [1]. A recommendation supported by the evidence, for example solar with a gas boiler as back-up on cloudy days [1].
